editorialScope: Owner-requested companion biography. Personal specimen records are separate from the main general-audience atlas. Undocumented ancient ownership and findspot remain unknown.

generationModel.meaning: Illustrative elapsed time, not a count of owners or custodians.

sources.title: Certification record: 2086328-049
sources.author: NGC
sources.scope: Records c.440–404 BC, Attica, Athens, AR tetradrachm; MS, strike 4/5, surface 4/5; grade date 12 October 2018.
sources.note: The field titled Pedigree contains a design description, not former owners. The grade date is not a discovery date. Owner-supplied holder photographs corroborate the label; no new authentication is claimed.

sources.title: Auction 1224867 · 2 October 2022
sources.author: GreatCollections
sources.scope: Records certificate 2086328-049 and 17.21 g. Auction ended 2 October 2022 and is marked sold.
sources.note: Its title states strike 5/5, conflicting with the current NGC record, supplied holder photograph and 2024 listing. This inconsistency does not establish a regrade. Price requires login and is not reported here.

sources.title: Auction 1594499 · 9 June 2024
sources.author: GreatCollections
sources.scope: Records certificate 2086328-049, 17.21 g, MS, strike 4/5 and surface 4/5. Auction ended 9 June 2024 and is marked sold.
sources.note: The certification number links the record to the specimen. No buyer, later transfer, invoice settlement or continuous ownership chain is established. Price requires login.

sources.title: Athenian tetradrachm · Acropolis hoard 1886, no. 20
sources.author: Acropolis Museum
sources.scope: An owl dated 483–480 BC from a hoard found on the Acropolis in 1886. A documented example of a coin with a recorded hoard context.
sources.note: This is an earlier, different specimen. Its findspot and preservation history cannot be transferred to NGC 2086328-049. No museum photograph is reproduced on the companion page.

sources.title: Identifying Archaeological Metal · CCI Notes 4/1
sources.author: Canadian Conservation Institute
sources.scope: Explains how metal and burial environments affect corrosion, including silver corrosion products.
sources.note: General preservation context, not a diagnosis of this specimen or evidence that it was buried.

sources.title: Life of Augustus, chapter 75
sources.author: Suetonius; translated by J. C. Rolfe
sources.scope: Describes Augustus giving old royal coins and foreign money as festive gifts. Supports interest in older or unusual coins in antiquity.
sources.note: Does not establish an ancient collector’s involvement in this owl’s survival or an organized modern-style collecting tradition. Translation published in 1913.

sources.title: The Beni Hasan Coin-Hoard
sources.author: J. Grafton Milne
sources.scope: Journal of Egyptian Archaeology 19 (1933), pp. 119–121. Describes 54 Athenian-type tetradrachms as exceptionally preserved and apparently uncirculated.
sources.note: The opening primary text was checked in an indexed scan; the complete page image could not be retrieved. Historical condition language is not a modern grade. The article considers an Egyptian origin for these pieces; they are not identified as the featured coin or its hoard.

sources.title: Collecting Money · The Value of Money
sources.author: Smithsonian National Museum of American History
sources.scope: Places the recognizable collecting hobby in the Renaissance and notes possible ancient Roman precedents.
sources.note: Ancient appreciation and the later organized hobby are distinct. The exhibit does not establish a unique first collector or this specimen’s ownership.

sources.title: His Audience with the Emperor · Familiar Letters XIX.3
sources.author: Francesco Petrarch; translation edited by James Harvey Robinson and Henry Winchester Rolfe
sources.scope: Petrarch recounts giving treasured ancient Roman gold and silver coins to Charles IV as examples of rulers to emulate. See pp. 370–376, especially 371–372.
sources.note: The page uses a broad fourteenth-century date to distinguish the 1354 encounter from the 1355 letter. These Roman coins are not the Athenian owl pictured here. No claim that Petrarch was the first collector.

sources.title: History of the Department of Coins, Medals and Antiques
sources.author: Bibliothèque nationale de France
sources.scope: Describes Louis XIV expanding the royal Cabinet and moving it to Versailles so he could spend time with it daily; the collection is ancestral to the BnF department.
sources.note: The Cabinet contained antiquities as well as coins. This institutional history supports the royal-collector setting, not any royal ownership of NGC 2086328-049.

fiction.title: The gift that waited.
fiction.status: Explicitly labeled historical fiction, requested by the owner. Not specimen provenance.
fiction.limits: No most/usually claim about high-grade survival rates. No named historical collector is connected to this specimen. The long pause and later collecting are one imagined possibility.
